name: Lakehouse catalogs
summary: The service every engine asks “where is this table right now?”: it maps table names to their current metadata, makes commits atomic, and decides who may read which files.
howItWorks: An Iceberg table is a pile of immutable files plus a chain of metadata files, and only one of those metadata files is current. The catalog stores that pointer for each name, such as `sales.orders` → `s3://lake/…/00042-….metadata.json`, grouped into namespaces (also called databases or schemas). To commit, a writer writes new data and a new metadata file, then asks the catalog to swap the pointer from the version it started on to its new one. The swap is a compare-and-swap: if another writer got there first, the catalog refuses, and the writer rebuilds its commit on top of the newer version and tries again. Readers just load whatever the pointer says. Most catalogs now speak the same Iceberg REST protocol, so Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB and PyIceberg can share one catalog. A REST catalog can also hand each client short-lived storage credentials scoped to one table’s folder (credential vending), so the catalog’s grants decide who can read the files and engines never hold bucket-wide keys. Catalogs differ in how much they own: for an external table the catalog only records a location you chose, and dropping it leaves the files; for a managed table the catalog picks the location, maintains the files and deletes them when the table is dropped.
analogy: A library’s front desk. The books sit on open shelves, but the desk knows which edition of each title is the current one, stamps a new edition in only if nobody beat you to it, and gives each reader a pass that opens just the shelves they’re allowed to browse.
useWhen: More than one engine reads or writes the same open-format tables, such as Spark for ETL, Trino for dashboards and DuckDB in notebooks
You want one place to grant and revoke table access, enforced by vended credentials instead of per-engine copies of the rules and bucket keys
Several writers commit to the same tables and need conflicts caught instead of silently overwriting each other
You’d rather let the platform choose file locations, compact files and clean up after drops (managed tables)
avoidWhen: One tool reads a few Parquet files; a catalog adds a service, a database behind it and an auth setup for nothing
Engines that bypass the catalog with their own bucket credentials; its grants then protect nothing, so lock down the storage first

Expecting the catalog to keep tables tidy: Polaris runs no maintenance, Lakekeeper’s snapshot expiry and orphan-file removal come only in its paid Lakekeeper+ edition and are off by default, and neither compacts files, so plan your own jobs
example: A retailer keeps 400 Iceberg tables in one S3 bucket. Spark jobs write them every 15 minutes, analysts query them from Trino, and data scientists open them in DuckDB. All three point at one REST catalog. When an analyst runs a query on `sales.orders`, Trino asks the catalog for the table, gets the location of its current metadata file plus S3 credentials that only cover that table’s prefix and expire within an hour, and reads the files directly. Two Spark jobs that try to commit to the same table in the same second can’t both win: the catalog accepts one and the other retries on top of it. Revoking the analysts’ grant stops their next table load in every engine at once; credentials already handed out keep working until they expire.

sections.title: Managed and external tables
sections.intro: The same split exists in Hive, Unity Catalog and most other catalogs. The question is who owns the files’ location and lifecycle; the files stay in your storage either way.

rows.label: Who picks the location
values: The catalog, under a storage root set on the catalog, schema or warehouse
You, with a `LOCATION` clause or path that the catalog records

rows.label: Who may change the files
values: Only the catalog’s own write path; Hive warns that changing them behind its back can cause undefined behavior, and Unity Catalog doesn’t allow path-based access
You and any tool with access to the path; Unity Catalog doesn’t enforce its grants on direct file access

rows.label: What `DROP TABLE` does
values: Deletes the data too. Hive moves it to the trash unless you add `PURGE`; Databricks deletes the files after a recovery period (7 days by default) during which `UNDROP` brings the table back
Removes only the catalog entry; the files stay until you delete them

rows.label: Maintenance
values: The platform can do it: Databricks’ predictive optimization runs `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM` and `ANALYZE`; S3 Tables compacts and expires snapshots by default
Yours: compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup are your jobs

rows.label: Formats
values: What the catalog can manage: Delta Lake or Iceberg in Unity Catalog, Iceberg in S3 Tables
Anything the engines can read: in Unity Catalog also CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet, ORC and text

rows.label: Pick it when
values: The catalog’s engines are the main writers and you want optimization and cleanup handled
Other systems already write the files at a fixed path, or the format isn’t one the catalog manages

notes: Databricks recommends managed tables by default and offers `ALTER TABLE … SET MANAGED` to convert external Delta tables in place. Its other docs page gives the drop retention as 8 days; the managed-tables page says 7 days, configurable to 0 or 7 to 30 days.

sections.title: Catalogs you’ll meet
sections.intro: Most of these answer the Iceberg REST protocol, so an engine configured for one can usually talk to another.

items.name: Hive Metastore
items.text: Hive’s system catalog, described in 2009: databases as namespaces, and for each table its columns, location and format, usually kept in a relational database. Iceberg’s `HiveCatalog` stores the current metadata file as the table property `metadata_location`, and many catalogs still offer a Hive-compatible API.

items.name: AWS Glue Data Catalog
items.text: AWS’s central metadata store for Athena, EMR and Glue, with an Iceberg REST endpoint at `https://glue.<region>.amazonaws.com/iceberg`. Lake Formation adds grants and vends temporary S3 credentials.

items.name: Amazon S3 Tables
items.text: A bucket type that is its own Iceberg catalog: S3 picks the file locations and runs compaction, snapshot management and unreferenced-file removal.

items.name: Lakehouse runtime catalog
items.text: A serverless metastore for Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage, called BigLake metastore until 20 April 2026. It speaks Iceberg REST and vends short-lived tokens.

items.name: Unity Catalog
items.text: Databricks’ governance layer, with managed and external tables and volumes, an Iceberg REST endpoint and credential vending. An Apache 2.0 open-source version is a sandbox project at LF AI & Data.

items.name: Apache Polaris
items.text: A full Iceberg REST catalog with role-based access control and credential vending, built by Snowflake and a top-level Apache project since February 2026.

items.name: Lakekeeper
items.text: An Iceberg REST catalog shipped as a single Rust binary, with OpenFGA authorization, credential vending or remote signing, and change events. Maintained by Vakamo.

items.name: Project Nessie and Apache Gravitino
items.text: Nessie is a transactional catalog with Git-like branches. Gravitino federates metadata from many sources and runs an Iceberg REST service; it became a top-level Apache project in June 2025.

story: Hive, built at Facebook and described in a 2009 VLDB paper, brought a system catalog to Hadoop. Its metastore held each table’s columns, format and directory, with databases as namespaces, and lived in a relational database such as MySQL, or a local file system, because HDFS was built for sequential scans, not small random updates. The catalog said where a table lived, but the files in its directories were the truth, and Hive’s paper admitted it had to keep metadata and data consistent by hand. Hive also splits tables into managed ones, whose files it owns and deletes on `DROP`, and external ones, whose files it only points at.

Iceberg turned the catalog into the commit point. Its spec keeps a table’s whole state in metadata files and makes a commit one atomic swap of a pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, implemented with a check-and-put in a metastore or database. Any store that could do that worked: the Hive Metastore, AWS Glue, a JDBC database, Nessie. Every engine then needed a client for every catalog, so in July 2022 Iceberg 0.14 added a common REST catalog client, with commits sent as changes that the service checks for conflicts.

The REST protocol became the common interface. In June and July 2024 Databricks open-sourced Unity Catalog and Snowflake open-sourced Polaris, and Gravitino entered the Apache Incubator the same June; all three speak Iceberg REST. The clouds offer their own Iceberg REST endpoints too: AWS Glue and S3 Tables, Google’s BigLake metastore (renamed the Lakehouse runtime catalog in April 2026) and Microsoft’s OneLake. With the formats open, the fight moved to the catalog: who governs access, who maintains the files, and whose engines can write.

choices.choice: Keep the catalog small: one pointer per table
choices.why: Object stores can’t atomically replace a file or list a directory consistently, but a database can update one row with a check. Putting only the pointer in the catalog keeps the data and the full metadata in open files that any engine can read.
Writers prepare everything first and only ask the catalog to swap at the end. A conflict costs a retry, not a lock that a crashed job could hold forever, and readers are never blocked.

choices.choice: A REST protocol instead of a client per catalog
choices.why: The Hive, Glue, JDBC and Nessie catalogs each needed their own client code in every engine. One HTTP protocol means one client per engine, with commits sent as changes and conflicts resolved on the service side.
Grants in a catalog mean little if every engine holds keys to the whole bucket. Returning short-lived credentials scoped to one table with each load lets one set of rules govern every engine.
